Odin × Godot

Authoring guide — the Odin script feature reference

51 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
API conventions shared by Kit and ReplaySingle-file authoringAnatomy of a scriptReserved procedure signatures and fieldsManual overridesGenerated namesMultiplayer RPCs (@(gd_rpc))Godot helper proceduresSupported Odin → Variant typesThreads & memoryBuildingMultiple scripts in one packageCustom resourcesGlobal class namesTyped cross-script referencesAutoload singletonsEditor tooling

This reference covers the Odin script struct convention, //gd: markers, @export forms, lifecycle callbacks, methods, signals, resources, autoloads, cross-script access, gd.* helpers, and editor tooling. Start with Getting Started for setup and a first script. For the build, edit, and debug loop, see Workflow.

Write <name>.odin using the struct and procedure conventions below. The scriptgen preprocessor, run by build/build_scripts.sh, reads its tags and markers and generates registration code, including Variant argument wrappers, backing arrays, and @(init) registration. The authored and generated files compile together into the scripts library. Edit the authored source.

API conventions shared by Kit and Replay#

Use Odin's naming and style conventions: Ada_Case for types and enum members, snake_case for procedures and fields, and SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE for constants. Prefer a short, meaningful import alias. Indent with four spaces and put each statement on its own line; make format applies this layout. Use explicit error handling in examples. Generated Godot bindings retain their existing engine-derived names, such as gd.Node2d and gd.node2d_set_position.

Script helpers use the snake-case script type as their prefix: Player_Controller and the existing PlayerController spelling both produce player_controller_*; HUD_View produces hud_view_*. A lifecycle proc is therefore player_controller_ready; an exposed player_controller_jump method appears as jump to Godot. Two script types in one package must have distinct snake-case prefixes. Regenerate scripts after changing a type name. Existing acronym spellings that depended on one underscore per capital must migrate to the whole-word prefix, such as http_server_* for HTTPServer.

Rule Kit (v1) Replay (v2)
Normal game loop Generated <game>_net_attach, <game>_net_frame, <game>_net_detach session_open, session_frame, session_close; use Room when authority can migrate
Gameplay mutation Tagged fields and generated command wrappers A typed value World and model step/action callbacks
Presentation Generated event handlers and typed entity queries Drain all presentation changes, then present copied state
Additional mechanisms Raw session/lane/transport APIs for custom integrations Raw net/P2P/transport APIs for custom policies

Choose one top-level runtime to drive the game. Kit's generated network callbacks, Replay Session, and Replay Room each advance their lower layers; do not also advance those layers yourself. Keep live owners at stable addresses and pass them by pointer. Configuration and copied World/frame values may be copied; live owners with allocations, callbacks or connections may not. Start configuration from the documented defaults, rather than assuming every empty options struct is usable.

Match setup and teardown: init/destroy for owned Odin storage, open/close for a live session, and attach/detach for an engine attachment. Packages with several owners add a type prefix, such as session_open. These verbs describe ownership. In a Godot script, release live owners in *_exit_tree. A defer in *_ready would run when that callback returns, not when the node leaves the tree. Borrowed readers, handles and views do not acquire ownership merely by being returned from a procedure. A query may return copied values, an owner-borrowed slice, or a frame-temporary view of live entity handles. Check its lifetime before retaining a result. Initialization can allocate diagnostics even when it fails; perform the documented cleanup on failure too. Fixed-value World components such as Pool and owned state need no independent destructor.

The ordinary call sequence is setup, frame/service, drain, read, teardown. Queries read current state; frame/service calls advance it; queue consumers must drain until empty. Configuration fields and documented observations form the supported API of a runtime owner. Its other fields are storage for the implementation, not another way to drive it.

Successful action or chat submission can mean that work was queued locally. Use the authoritative receipt or confirmed presentation change when game logic needs an accepted outcome; a successful send alone does not establish it.

See Kit conventions and the Replay starting path for each model's concrete lifetimes, defaults and extension points.

Single-file authoring#

There is one file per script: the .odin you write is also the resource you attach to a node. Put your scripts under the project (e.g. res://scripts/foo.odin) and attach res://scripts/foo.odin directly in the scene. The loader reads its canonical resource path and binds it to the descriptor generated for that exact file. //gd:class is optional and only adds a Godot global-class alias. There is no separate "resource stub" file to keep in sync.

Each scripts directory gets one odin_godot_scripts.gen.odin beside its sources, with a marked section for each script. The generated file must share the directory's package. The loader ignores *.gen.odin, so generated files are not attachable scripts. The editor hides them from the FileSystem dock by default.

Anatomy of a script#

Odin
//gd:extends Node          // base Godot class. Optional — derived from `owner` when omitted.
//gd:class Ping            // optional: opt into Godot's global class namespace
//gd:tool                  // optional: registers as a @tool script
package my_scripts

import gd "godot:godot"

// The script struct's first field must be the owner Object handle. The core
// writes the owner pointer at offset 0. Choose the handle type used by your
// procedures (gd.Node, gd.Object, gd.Node2d, ...). The base follows
// //gd:extends when present; otherwise it is derived from the handle type.
Ping :: struct {
	owner:  gd.Node,
	pinged: gd.Signal1(int) `gd:"args=value"`, // signal field -> declared signal (see Signals)
	speed:  f32    `gd:"export"`,  // tagged field -> @export var
	count:  gd.Int `gd:"export"`,
	scratch: int,                 // untagged -> private per-instance state
}

// Engine calls (add_child, connect_to, queue_free, ...) take `self.owner`.
// `self` points to this Odin struct. Engine handles are distinct types,
// so the compiler rejects a script pointer passed as an engine handle.
// scriptgen also rejects the bare-`self` form at build time
// ("...is the ^Ping script struct, not an engine object — pass self.owner").

// Lifecycle procs: matched by name (after stripping an optional `<struct>_`
// prefix) against ready / process / physics_process / enter_tree / exit_tree, and
// bound by the `^Ping` receiver. Write a plain Odin proc; codegen wraps it.
ping_ready :: proc(self: ^Ping) {
	if self.speed == 0 {self.speed = 1.5}
}

// Custom methods: tag with @(gd_method). Callable from GDScript. The exposed name
// is the proc name minus the `<struct>_` prefix (`ping_add` -> `add`). Codegen
// generates the Variant trampoline from the typed signature.
@(gd_method)
ping_add :: proc(self: ^Ping, a, b: int) -> int {return a + b}

@(gd_method)
ping_emit_ping :: proc(self: ^Ping, value: int) {
	self.count += gd.Int(value)
	ping_emit_pinged(self, i64(value))   // generated emit helper (see below)
}

Markers (//gd: comments)#

Marker Meaning
//gd:extends <Class> The Godot base class. Optional: when omitted, it is derived from the owner field's type.
//gd:class <Name> Optional Godot global-class alias, like GDScript class_name. Runtime attachment does not need it.
//gd:tool Registers the class as a @tool script (is_tool() == true) and runs in the editor.
//gd:icon res://path.svg Custom class icon (Scene dock, Create Node/Resource dialog).
//gd:group a b Declarative group membership: every instance joins the named groups on READY (space-separated, repeatable). Replaces gd.add_to_group boilerplate in _ready; pairs with the typed group queries (rt.scripts_in_group & co.).

The authored res://scripts/<x>.odin path is the runtime identity. Markers add engine metadata and behavior; they do not decide which compiled descriptor attaches. Several scripts may therefore share a base type, or a struct name across separate Odin packages, because their resource paths distinguish them.

//gd:extends and the owner field state the same fact twice, so scriptgen cross-checks them. The owner handle must be the declared base or one of its ancestors.

Odin
//gd:extends CharacterBody2D
Player :: struct { owner: gd.Node2d }   // fine — a wider handle; the script only calls Node2D methods

//gd:extends Node
Player :: struct { owner: gd.Node2d }   // build error — a NARROWER handle

A narrower handle lets a script call methods its Godot base does not support. Class handles share the distinct gd.Object representation, so Odin accepts a gd.Node2d handle even when the registered class is a plain Node. A gd.node2d_* call through that handle can then crash inside Godot. The build error names the declared base, the handle type, and the two ways to make them consistent.

Omit the marker to derive the base from the handle type:

Odin
//gd:class Coin
package scripts
Coin :: struct { owner: gd.Area2d }     // registers as Area2D

The base falls back to Node only where the handle can't be placed (no -godot: root, or a type that isn't a ClassDB class), and the check stays silent in exactly those cases.

The tag vocabulary#

Every `gd:"…"` tag starts with a token selecting the field kind. The table below follows FIELD_TOKENS in decl/decl.odin, the schema shared by scriptgen and the runtime reflection registrar:

First token What it declares Consumed by In the wire fingerprint
export an editor-visible property the runtime registrar no
onready=PATH an auto-wired node reference (^ScriptStruct field: node + typed script struct) the runtime registrar no
replicate a networked field on the DELTA lane (kit/net) scriptgen yes
owner a networked field streamed from its owning peer scriptgen yes
predict a networked field the sim predicts and reconciles (kit/sim) scriptgen yes
backup a field the session backup carries scriptgen no (see below)
manual "I call the generated thing myself" scriptgen no
profile=T the per-player profile row type scriptgen yes
entity=Name:id a spawnable entity type and its stable id both yes

args=a,b follows the first token and names a signal payload's parameters. "In the wire fingerprint" means the declaration contributes to NET_FINGERPRINT. Peers compare that fingerprint at join and reject mismatched builds before interpreting gameplay packets.

backup is excluded from the session fingerprint. Its codec checks a fnv1a32 format stamp when loading a save and rejects an incompatible format. That check is separate from network admission: peers with different save formats can still play together if their network declarations agree. The table marks a declaration yes when peers must agree on its wire representation.

A declaration that contributes to NET_FINGERPRINT selects the field kind and must be the tag's first token. backup and manual also lead their tags, though they do not contribute to the fingerprint. The selected kind determines which options may follow:

  • replicate, owner, and predict each select one lane with its own allowed options, listed below. slack= belongs to the predicted lane. Combining owner with predict, or using slack= outside predict, is invalid.
  • entity=Name:id declares a permanent public type id and an entry in the factory table. Scriptgen makes the field an exported PackedScene, so write `gd:"entity=Mob:3"` rather than `gd:"export,resource=PackedScene,entity=Mob:3"`. Follow it with entity options: stream_hz=N sets the kind's owner-stream rate for every peer and spawn, and avatar marks a seat's body so a host takeover parks it with the seat instead of adopting it. Export specifications can follow, as in entity=Mob:3,stream_hz=30,group=Spawns. See kit/boot.
Lane Tag Its options
delta gd:"replicate" interp, interp=angle, interp=BLEND_PROC, wire=f16, wire=CODEC
owner-streamed gd:"owner" continuous stock types interpolate by default; snap opts out; interp=angle, interp=BLEND_PROC, wire=f16, wire=CODEC customize
predicted gd:"predict" the above, plus slack=N, glide=N, cut=N

_edge halves pair with gd:"replicate" fields and discrete owner fields. Predicted state uses resimulation, and continuous owner-streamed state uses interpolation, so those fields have separate presentation paths.

A field's resolved lane is what folds into NET_FINGERPRINT, so two builds that resolve a field to the same lane share a session bit for bit regardless of how the tag is spelled. A field selects one lane. The deprecated combined spelling gd:"replicate,interp,owner,wire=f16" is refused at build time, with the error naming its replacement, gd:"owner,wire=f16" (continuous owner fields interpolate automatically).

Exports#

Struct fields tagged `gd:"export"` become @export vars: the field name is the property name, the field type maps to a Variant type. offset/size are derived with offset_of / size_of, so the core narrows native Variant widths (Int=i64, Float=f64) to your field's real width (e.g. f32).

Export fields use the supported Godot Variant types below. Use a gd.<Type> binding type or a bare Odin scalar, which the runtime narrows to the field's width:

Category Field types
Scalars bool; i8/i16/i32/i64/int/u8/u16/u32/u64/uint/gd.Int; f32/f64/gd.Float
Strings gd.String, gd.String_Name, gd.Node_Path
Math gd.Vector2/Vector2i, gd.Rect2/Rect2i, gd.Vector3/Vector3i, gd.Vector4/Vector4i, gd.Transform2d/Transform3d, gd.Plane, gd.Quaternion, gd.Aabb, gd.Basis, gd.Projection, gd.Color
Containers gd.Dictionary, gd.Array, and every gd.Packed_*_Array (Byte, Int32, Int64, Float32, Float64, String, Vector2, Vector3, Vector4, Color)
Handles Resource handles such as gd.Texture2d and pointers to them; gd.Object with an explicit resource= hint; gd.Rid (see below)

Note: gd.Callable/gd.Signal/gd.Rid map to their Variant types but are not meaningfully editable in the Inspector (Godot itself doesn't expose them as exports); prefer them only for cross-script data, not for editor-tunable values. An unrecognized field type is a hard scriptgen: error: (so a typo is never silently an Object).

Extend the tag with a hint specification: `gd:"export,SPEC"`. Top-level tokens are comma-separated; values within a specification are colon-separated (so a file filter's commas never collide) and are rewritten to Godot's comma-joined hint_string form:

Tag Inspector widget Godot hint / hint_string
gd:"export,range=0:100" numeric slider Range / "0,100"
gd:"export,range=0:100:5" slider with step Range / "0,100,5"
gd:"export,enum=Idle:Walk:Run" named-int dropdown Enum / "Idle,Walk,Run"
gd:"export,multiline" multi-line text box Multiline_Text
gd:"export,file" file picker (any) File / ""
gd:"export,file=*.png:*.jpg" filtered file picker File / "*.png,*.jpg"
gd:"export,dir" directory picker Dir
gd:"export,global_file" / global_dir global file/dir picker Global_File / Global_Dir
gd:"export,resource=Texture2D" typed resource picker Resource_Type / "Texture2D"
gd:"export,array=int" typed-array editor Type_String / "2:"
gd:"export,array=Texture2D" typed-array of resources Type_String / "24/17:Texture2D"
gd:"export,dict=String;int" typed-dictionary editor Type_String / "4:;2:"
gd:"export,dict=String;Texture2D" typed-dict, resource values Type_String / "4:;24/17:Texture2D"

resource= is for an Object/resource-handle field; range/enum for an int or float; multiline for a gd.String. A typed resource handle derives its own resource= hint. Prefer bullet_scene: gd.Packed_Scene `` gd:"export"``: the build reads the class from the type, the Inspector shows a PackedScene picker, andgd.instantiate(self.bullet_scene)` needs no cast.

Write resource= explicitly only for a type-erased gd.Object field. Object exports require a resource hint, whether derived or explicit, so the runtime can retain the assigned resource. Without a hint, the scene loader could drop its reference and leave a dangling pointer; the build rejects that declaration. Node handles such as gd.Node2d or ^gd.Node2d cannot be exported. Use onready= to reference scene nodes. array=ELEM (on a gd.Array field) and dict=KEY;VALUE (on a gd.Dictionary field) declare typed collections, the same Inspector editors that GDScript's Array[T] / Dictionary[K,V] produce. Each element/key/value is a builtin (int, float, String, Vector2, Color, …) or a Resource class name (Texture2D, PackedScene, …). Each field accepts at most one hint. For a scene used to spawn a network entity, gd:"entity=Name:id" generates both the export and the resource=PackedScene hint. See Entities and the <game>_entities factory in kit/boot.

Odin
Probe :: struct {
	owner:       gd.Node,
	health:      i32        `gd:"export,range=0:100:5"`,
	mode:        i32        `gd:"export,enum=Idle:Walk:Run"`,
	description: gd.String  `gd:"export,multiline"`,
	velocity:    gd.Vector3 `gd:"export"`,
	texture:     gd.Object  `gd:"export,resource=Texture2D"`,
	scores:      gd.Array   `gd:"export,array=int"`,            // Array[int]
	loot:        gd.Dictionary `gd:"export,dict=String;PackedScene"`, // Dictionary[String, PackedScene]
}

The values still live as untyped gd.Array / gd.Dictionary handles in Odin (you read/write them through the array_* / dictionary_* methods); the array=/dict= tag only drives the export's typing: the Inspector widget and the engine-side key/value type enforcement.

Alternatively, declare the field as gd.Typed_Array(T) or gd.Typed_Dictionary(K, V). A bare gd:"export" then derives the hint from the type:

Odin
scores: gd.Typed_Array(i64)                       `gd:"export"`,  // == array=int
loot:   gd.Typed_Dictionary(gd.String, gd.Packed_Scene) `gd:"export"`, // == dict=String;PackedScene

Element types are the Odin spellings (i64, gd.String, gd.Texture2d); Resource handles are mapped back to their engine class name automatically (gd.Texture2d → Texture2D). For acronym-heavy class names that don't round-trip cleanly (e.g. JSON, GLTFDocument), use the array=/dict= tag form with the exact name. Don't combine the two on one field: that's a build-time error.

Export groups & subgroups#

Add a group= (or subgroup=) token to an export to open a collapsible Inspector header that applies to that field and every export after it, until the next marker:

Odin
Player :: struct {
	owner:   gd.Character_Body2d,
	speed:   f32 `gd:"export,group=Movement"`, // "Movement" header starts here
	jump:    f32 `gd:"export"`,                 // …still under "Movement"
	hp:      i32 `gd:"export,group=Combat"`,    // "Combat" header starts here
	defense: i32 `gd:"export"`,                 // …under "Combat"
}

The marker is emitted as a PROPERTY_USAGE_GROUP (or …_SUBGROUP) entry immediately before the field's own property entry, so the engine renders the header in both the live property list and the editor placeholder. The group's name-prefix is empty (property names are not auto-prefixed). group= and subgroup= combine with any hint/default/getter on the same field.

Export default values#

default= carries an initializer for a scalar export (int/float/bool/String). The value is applied to the field when the instance is created (after zeroing, before _ready) and reported through Godot's default-value API, so the Inspector shows it and the reset-to-default arrow works:

Odin
Player :: struct {
	owner: gd.Node,
	speed: f32       `gd:"export,default=200"`,
	name:  gd.String `gd:"export,default=Hero"`,
	alive: bool      `gd:"export,default=true"`,
}

Only scalar Variant types support default=: numbers, bool, and String. The reflection registrar reports default= on a math-struct or handle field in the editor's output at boot, after scriptgen has run. Set those values in _ready or in the scene instead. The following table explains when each validation check runs.

Export validation at build and registration#

Both scriptgen and the runtime reflection registrar read `gd:"export,…"` tags. They validate different parts of the declaration:

Tier When What it checks How a failure looks
scriptgen build the first token and each specification name that follows it scriptgen: error: player.odin:7: …, the build stops
the reflection registrar boot / class registration each specification's value type, hint arity, and required Variant type an error in Godot's output, the field registers with that spec dropped

The runtime uses the field's reflected Variant type to check whether array= has a gd.Array field or default=Hero has a compatible type rather than a Vector2. Scriptgen can check specification names earlier, so a misspelling stops the build:

Odin
hp: i32 `gd:"export,rnage=0:100"`
// scriptgen: error: Player.hp: unknown export spec "rnage" — did you mean `range`?

The recognized spec set is decl/decl.odin's EXPORT_SPECS, and tests/scriptgen asserts it against the registrar's own switches, so the two tiers agree on which names exist.

Getter / setter properties#

Route an export's reads/writes through Odin procs (for validation, clamping, or side-effects) with get=/set=. The named procs take ^<Struct> plus (for the setter) the field value, and run instead of the raw field access from both GDScript and the editor:

Odin
Player :: struct {
	owner: gd.Node,
	hp:    i32 `gd:"export,get=player_get_hp,set=player_set_hp"`,
}

// reads of `hp` return this; writes are clamped into [0,100].
player_get_hp :: proc(self: ^Player) -> i32 { return self.hp }
player_set_hp :: proc(self: ^Player, v: i32) { self.hp = clamp(v, 0, 100) }

The get/set procs are plain Odin procedures (no @(gd_method) needed) named exactly as written in the tag. The backing field still exists: the getter/setter may use it as storage (as above) or compute from other state. Combine them with group=/default= (a defaulted getter/setter field applies its default through the setter).

@onready node references#

A struct field tagged `gd:"onready=PATH"` is auto-wired to a child node on _ready, mirroring GDScript's @onready var sprite = $Sprite. On the node's READY (before any @(gd_connect) wiring and your own _ready proc), the core resolves get_node(owner, "PATH") and writes the result into the field before your _ready runs:

Odin
Player :: struct {
	owner:  gd.Character_Body2d,
	sprite: gd.Node2d `gd:"onready=Sprite"`,    // owner-relative node path
	label:  gd.Node   `gd:"onready=HUD/Label"`,
}

The field must be an object/node handle (gd.Node2d, gd.Sprite2D, gd.Object, …). The handle contains the node pointer, so use the bare handle type, not ^gd.Node2d. An @onready field is a private reference resolved at runtime. It is not serialized or shown in the property list or Inspector.

When the field type is ^<script struct>, the core resolves the node and its typed Odin script struct using the same checks as rt.script_of. One declaration replaces a separate node handle and rt.script_of call in _ready:

Odin
Player :: struct {
	owner: gd.Character_Body2d,
	hud:   ^Hud `gd:"onready=HudLayer/Hud"`,   // node -> ^Hud, wired before _ready
}

// instead of:
//   hud_control: gd.Control `gd:"onready=HudLayer/Hud"`,
//   hud_script:  ^Hud,                          // + rt.script_of in _ready

The pointee must be a script struct in the module; other types are a build error. If the node exists but carries no Hud script, the field stays nil and push_error names the field. After a changed-layout hot reload, the core re-resolves these declared references once every instance has migrated. A manually cached rt.script_of pointer would instead refer to the old storage.

A typed reference points to script data. Pass its .owner to engine calls, as in gd.canvas_item_set_visible(self.hud.owner, false). Passing the script reference itself is a compile error (Cannot assign value ... of type '^Hud' to 'Canvas_Item') because engine handles are distinct types.

For a fixed-array field, use [N]Handle or [N]^Script to resolve N sibling nodes in one declaration. The path holds exactly one %d, substituted with 0-based indices at READY:

Odin
Shop :: struct {
	owner:   gd.Control,
	cards:   [9]gd.Button `gd:"onready=Grid/Card%d"`,   // Grid/Card0 … Grid/Card8
	choices: [3]^Choice   `gd:"onready=Panel/Choice%d"`, // typed script refs work too
}

Each element resolves independently (a missing index leaves that slot nil with the engine's path error); a %d on a scalar field — or an array without one — is a build error. This replaces separate numbered fields (card0, card1, …) and a manual lookup loop in _ready.

Godot's scene-unique %Name syntax works in any onready= path. Check Access as Unique Name on the node, as for GDScript's $ %Name lookup. The marker passes through to get_node, so the path can start at the unique node:

Odin
Player :: struct {
	owner: gd.Character_Body2d,
	hud:   ^Hud       `gd:"onready=%Hud"`,          // unique name, anywhere in the scene
	ammo:  gd.Label   `gd:"onready=%Hud/AmmoLabel"`, // unique segment, then a normal path
	slots: [4]gd.Button `gd:"onready=%Inv/Slot%d"`,  // combines with the array template
}

Only a % at a segment start (path start or right after /) is the unique-name marker; the array template's %d is recognized mid-name only (Slot%d), so a unique name that itself starts with d (%dock) is never mistaken for a template. Any other mid-name % is a build error. Unique names resolve through the owning scene's registry, so they follow the same scoping rules as GDScript's %Name.

Lifecycle & methods#

Both are plain Odin procs whose first parameter is ^<Struct>:

  • Lifecycle: the proc name (minus an optional <struct>_ prefix) is one of ready, process, physics_process, enter_tree, exit_tree, reload. process / physics_process take a delta: f64 second parameter.
  • Methods: tagged @(gd_method). Any name; exposed minus the struct prefix.

reload — the hot-reload hook#

<struct>_reload(self: ^T) runs with the new code after a hot reload swaps the scripts library. Reloads occur on editor save-on-rebuild or an explicit script.reload(true) in a running game. A same-layout reload preserves the struct in place and redirects engine entry points (_process, methods, signals) to the new code.

Stored procedure values still point into the old library. These include a callback or dispatch table, an events.Event, or a behaviour-tree node such as flow.Action.Call.fn. Reflection detects procedure-bearing state recursively. Rebuild that state in reload:

Odin
boss_reload :: proc(self: ^Boss) {
    self.behaviour = build_behaviour_tree()  // re-capture fresh proc pointers
}

After the reload hook returns, no state or external registration may call the previous library generation. The core releases the instance's lease on that generation and unloads it once no live instance retains it.

If reflection detects procedure-bearing or opaque rawptr state without a hook, the instance stays on its old code and retains that generation. A warning identifies the script that needs a hook. Other instances and intermediate generations continue reloading normally.

Reflection cannot see a callback erased inside an engine Callable/Variant container or registered with an external library without being stored in the struct. Those cases carry the same contract: define reload, remove/replace the old registration there, and never allow the old callback to survive the hook.

This only matters for scripts that run in the editor (//gd:tool) or are explicitly reloaded at runtime and retain callbacks. Ordinary gameplay scripts never hit it because a running game does not hot-reload itself.

Codegen wraps each in the proc "c" form the runtime expects, establishing a heap-backed default context before calling your proc, so your proc body can use ordinary Odin (allocations, etc.).

Signals#

Declare a signal as a struct field of one of the gd.Signal0 … gd.Signal4 marker types, whose arity is the payload count. The field name is the signal name, the type parameters are the payload types, and the optional gd:"args=..." tag names the payload (comma-separated, one name per parameter, with omitted names synthesizing as arg0, arg1, …). No tag is required; the field is recognized by its type. Declared signals are reported through _get_script_signal_list, so GDScript and the editor see them.

Odin
Player :: struct {
	owner:          gd.Node2d,
	health_changed: gd.Signal1(int) `gd:"args=value"`, // health_changed(value: int)
	leveled_up:     gd.Signal0,                        // leveled_up()
	hit:            gd.Signal2(int, ^gd.Node2d) `gd:"args=amount,who"`,
	// ...
}

The payload types must be Variant-able, following the same rule as @export and @(gd_method) args (object/node handles present as Object). A signal field costs one nil pointer of instance size and is never read or written at runtime; it exists so the declaration is part of the type, checked by the compiler, and visible to reflection.

gd.SignalN accepts an inline struct describing any number of arguments. Its field names become the argument names; an args= tag on a SignalN field is a build error. Use it for 5+ payload arguments, beyond the arity family's cap, or to name arguments in the type declaration:

Odin
Enemy :: struct {
	owner: gd.Node2d,
	hit:   gd.SignalN(struct {
		amount: int,
		who:    ^gd.Node2d,
		pos:    gd.Vector2,
		crit:   bool,
		combo:  i64,
	}), // hit(amount, who, pos, crit, combo) — 5 named args
}

SignalN requires a payload struct. A single Variant-mappable type such as gd.SignalN(gd.Vector2) is rejected. For one payload value, either gd.Signal1(gd.Vector2) (name it with args=) or wrap it so the field name names it: gd.SignalN(struct { pos: gd.Vector2 }) → moved(pos: Vector2).

Emit with the generated typed helper <struct_snake>_emit_<field> (e.g. ping_emit_pinged(self, value)), which codegen emits from the signal field and which calls through gd.emit/gd.emit_args (returning the engine Error, which you may ignore):

Odin
player_emit_health_changed(self, i64(self.health))   // generated typed emitter

Connect a signal to a handler procedure marked @(gd_method) so the engine can dispatch to it. Use a helper call or declarative wiring:

Odin
// 1. Connect an emitter's signal to a target's method, from any script (gd.* helper):
gd.connect_to(player, "health_changed", self.owner, "on_health_changed")

// 2. Connect one of the Godot owner's signals to its own method:
gd.connect(self.owner, "body_entered", "collect")

// 3. Use @(gd_connect), shown below, instead of a _ready/connect call.

Declarative signal wiring (@(gd_connect))#

Tag a @(gd_method) procedure with @(gd_connect = "signal_name") to connect the Godot owner's signal_name to this method on READY. The connection happens before your own _ready runs (order: @onready field resolution → @(gd_connect) connections → your _ready).

Odin
// Connect the Godot owner's `body_entered` to `on_body` on READY.
@(gd_method, gd_connect = "body_entered")
enemy_on_body :: proc(self: ^Enemy, body: gd.Node2d) {
	if self.dead { return }
	player := rt.script_of(body, Player)    // typed cross-script (see below)
	if player != nil {
		player_take_damage(player, CONTACT_DAMAGE)
	}
}

@(gd_connect) implies the proc is a signal target, so it must also be a @(gd_method) (use @(gd_method, gd_connect = "...")). The signal must exist on the emitter (an engine signal like body_entered / area_entered, or one a script declared with a signal field).

Use @(gd_connect = "Path/To/Node:signal") to connect another node's signal to this method. The part before the last : is a node path resolved at READY exactly like an onready= ref (owner-relative, absolute /root/..., or .. — anything get_node takes), the part after is the signal:

Odin
// Connect the child turret's `fired` signal to the parent before _ready.
@(gd_method, gd_connect = "Turret/Barrel:fired")
tank_on_fired :: proc(self: ^Tank, heat: gd.Int) { ... }

Children ready before parents, so a child emitter's script (and its declared signals) exists by the time the parent connects. For a missing node or signal, the connection is skipped and push_error names the declaring class and method. Use gd.connect_to from _ready for emitters resolved at runtime, such as spawned scenes. (@(gd_connect) requires the -custom-attribute:gd_connect build flag, which build/build_scripts.sh passes for you.)

A single %d in the path connects a sequence of emitters to one handler. It probes Choice0, Choice1, … until the first missing index and binds each match's index as a trailing callable argument. The engine passes that index after the signal's own arguments on every dispatch:

Odin
// Connect Panel/Choice0..ChoiceN's `pressed` here; `idx` identifies the emitter.
@(gd_method, gd_connect = "Panel/Choice%d:pressed")
menu_on_choice :: proc(self: ^Menu, idx: gd.Int) {
	menu_pick(self, int(idx))
}

This lets pick0, pick1, and pick2 share a handler. Index 0 must exist; a declaration that connects nothing reports push_error.

Scene-unique names work in the path part too, with the same rules as onready= (segment-start % = unique-name marker, mid-name %d = the indexed template):

Odin
@(gd_method, gd_connect = "%SavePanel:saved")     // unique-name emitter
@(gd_method, gd_connect = "%Inv/Slot%d:pressed")  // unique prefix + indexed bank

Reserved procedure signatures and fields#

Some toolkit declarations depend on a parameter's name, position, or type, or on a script field's type. Changing those parts can change the generated behavior even when the Odin code still compiles. The following table lists these declarations and the result of changing them.

Shape Where it is legal What it means Effect of changing the declaration
first param self: ^<Class> every bound proc identifies the receiver class by type the parameter name may change; a type that no longer matches the class prevents binding
a pointer param immediately after the receiver @(gd_command) / @(gd_method) on an embedded block identifies the containing entity, called the wielder; scriptgen supplies self so the block can access it. The pointer is never a wire argument a pointer there on a direct command is a build error ("un-wire-able arg")
by: knet.Player_Id (after the receiver/wielder) @(gd_command) identifies the issuer; the framework supplies the resolved sender so the predicate does not need to trust a client-supplied identity under another name, the parameter is ordinary client-controlled wire data. Both the name and type are required; other wire args named by are refused
typed entity params before mine an @(gd_event) _fx proc concrete entities used by presentation; one is the inferred anchor, while several require anchor=PARAM. The anchor chooses the session or sim clock an unknown/non-entity anchor, ambiguous list, or entity outside the selected runtime is a build error
mine: bool an @(gd_event) body's _fx proc, and a tick's _fx half true on the anchor owner/source timeline, false on observers; audience policy can omit either side position and name are both checked; the error names the slot
tick: u64 @(gd_sample) (required, second), @(gd_step) (optional, second) the lane's tick number on a sample, a build error; on a step, the parameter is omitted
l: ^ksim.Lane generated fact announcement procedures reserve l for the lane parameter — an author arg named l is refused because the generated parameter would shadow it
a kit/boot Boot field on the script struct the game shell declares the four standard transport forwards (on_packet / on_peer_left / on_net_up / on_net_down) see the note below

A field declares the game shell when its type's qualifier resolves to an import of godot:kit/boot. Any import alias works, including kboot or boot, because scriptgen checks the import path. A Boot from a different package does not declare the shell.

Manual overrides#

To override one of the generated procedures below, define a procedure with the same name. Scriptgen then uses the authored implementation. There is no separate opt-out tag or configuration token.

Generated Yields to a hand-written…
census accessors: <entity>_ref, <entity>_of, <entity>_owned_by, <entity>_mine, <entity>_ids, <entity>_all, <entity>_despawn, <entity>_teleport, <entity>_spawn proc of that name
acceptance-test probes: probe_<entity>_count, probe_my_<entity>, probe_<entity>_<field> proc (or @(gd_method)) of that name
the four standard transport forwards @(gd_method) of that name

Scriptgen prints each override once per run:

Code
scriptgen: yielded: runner_of (census accessor — the hand-written proc of that name wins)

That line confirms an intended override took effect and, when you didn't intend one, tells you a procedure in your package already uses a generated name. Check it if a proc you meant to override (runner_of where the entity is Runner_Bot) seems to do nothing.

Announcement procedures generated by @(gd_event) cannot be overridden. An authored procedure with the same name is a build error requiring a rename. The generated procedure coordinates authority-only broadcasts, _fx execution on the causer's live pass with mine=true, execution on watching screens at the fact's tick with mine=false, and suppression during resimulation so reconciliation cannot announce the event again.

gd:"manual" suppresses an automatic call while retaining the generated procedure for game code to call. For an embedded simulation block's @(gd_tick), the block's state still joins the entity descriptor and its commands still join the command table, but the game chooses when and whether to call its tick. See kit/sim. The token is not limited to simulation: using manual where there is no generated procedure to call is a build error naming what scriptgen expected.

Generated names#

Generated wrappers, wire constants, and lifecycle hooks use different naming rules. Use the wrapper to issue an action and implement the matching hook to receive a callback.

Action policies. @(gd_command) is owner-only and non-predicted by default. Use knet.ACTION_OWNER_PREDICTED, knet.ACTION_ANY_SEAT, knet.ACTION_ANY_SEAT_PREDICTED, or knet.ACTION_AUTHORITY when the verb differs. Both co-op and sim descriptors carry the same typed knet.Action_Policy, and access is enforced before the verb predicate. A knet.Action_Policy{...} literal can additionally set max_args_bytes. Quoted comma-string command policies are rejected; use a typed preset or literal.

Every generated command wrapper returns knet.Action_Outcome. Most call sites use knet.command_ok(outcome) to test whether the action applied or was predicted. UI that needs the cause of an immediate refusal can inspect outcome.reason; the generated game-shell <game>_command_rejected half receives the final authority reason (Access, Rate, Malformed, Stale, Predicate, or Timeout) for both co-op and tick-scheduled verbs. Its model parameter distinguishes .Immediate from .Scheduled; no packet or pending table is required in game code.

A command declared directly on the entity keeps its procedure name with a _cmd suffix. A command from an embedded block includes its field path, so two blocks of the same type on one entity get distinct names:

Declaration Generated wrapper
@(gd_command) gunner_buy :: proc(self: ^Gunner, …) gunner_buy_cmd (i.e. <proc>_cmd)
@(gd_command) gun_fire :: proc(self: ^Gun, …), embedded as primary: Gun on Gunner gunner_primary_fire_cmd (i.e. <class>_<path>_<verb>_cmd)

The composed form's path is the field path, joined with _, so a block three levels down still lands on the entity that owns the net id. Both formulas can reach the same name, and when they do it is a build error naming both declarations rather than a silently unreachable verb.

Wire-id constants: prefixed and unprefixed. Command ids are class-prefixed (GUNNER_CMD_BUY, GUNNER_CMD_PRIMARY_FIRE); world-pass fact ids are not (FACT_ROUND_OVER), and neither is NET_FINGERPRINT. Commands are per-entity, so several classes in one package can declare a verb of the same name, and the class prefix keeps their constants apart. Facts and the fingerprint are module-wide: there is exactly one announcement procedure per event name across the package (a second is a build error, as is a u16 hash collision between two events), and exactly one fingerprint.

Call <entity>_spawn to create an entity. Implement <entity>_spawned to receive the framework's creation notification:

Name Who writes it Who calls it What it does
mob_spawn generated you the typed factory: you call it to bring a Mob into the world
mob_spawned you the framework the hook: it calls you once the Mob exists, on every peer

Calling mob_spawn(…) inside mob_spawned(…) creates an infinite spawn loop. An authored mob_spawn replaces the generated factory because the name is a census accessor; scriptgen prints yielded: mob_spawn. Check that line if spawning does not behave as expected. The other framework-called hook, <entity>_freed, also uses the -ed suffix.

These identifiers are keyed by the entity's target struct. Two entity= tags cannot name the same struct because that would generate its entity accessors twice.

Multiplayer RPCs (@(gd_rpc))#

This section covers Godot's native multiplayer APIs: @(gd_rpc) mirrors GDScript's @rpc and supports MultiplayerSpawner/MultiplayerSynchronizer interoperation. Use these APIs when porting an RPC design or communicating with non-Odin peers. For a new cooperative game, the Kit multiplayer toolkit provides replicated fields, predicted commands with typed _then consequences, entity factories, joining, reconnect, and host migration. The game still defines its state and gameplay rules. See the tutorial, examples/cavecrawl, and examples/slopball. examples/coop_arena and examples/survivors demonstrate the native RPC APIs below.

Mark a @(gd_method) proc with @(gd_rpc) to expose it to Godot's high-level multiplayer, exactly like GDScript's @rpc(...) annotation. The annotation only declares the config; the engine routes node.rpc("method", args) (and incoming remote calls) to your proc through the same dispatch path as a normal method call.

Odin
//gd:extends Node
//gd:class Player
package game

import gd "godot:godot"

Player :: struct {
	owner:  gd.Node,
	health: gd.Int `gd:"export"`,
}

// Bare form: all defaults — authority mode, reliable, no call_local, channel 0.
@(gd_method, gd_rpc)
player_ping :: proc(self: ^Player) { /* runs when the authority RPCs us */ }

// Explicit config (comma-separated tokens, any order):
@(gd_method, gd_rpc = "any_peer,unreliable,call_local,channel=2")
player_take_damage :: proc(self: ^Player, amount: gd.Int) {
	self.health -= amount
}

gd_rpc implies gd_method: an RPC must be a registered, name-dispatchable method, so you can write @(gd_rpc) alone. Both forms are equivalent.

Config tokens and SDK defaults:

Token Effect Default
authority / any_peer who may call it (RPCMode) authority
reliable / unreliable / unreliable_ordered transfer mode reliable
call_local the RPC also runs on the calling peer off
channel=N transfer channel 0

Codegen exposes this configuration through _get_rpc_config, which the engine reads once per node. From GDScript or another script, call the method as usual:

GDScript
# A multiplayer peer must be active (e.g. ENetMultiplayerPeer or, for a single-process
# loopback, OfflineMultiplayerPeer):
node.multiplayer.multiplayer_peer = ENetMultiplayerPeer.new()  # ...create_server / _client
node.rpc("take_damage", 10)   # routed to player_take_damage on the configured peer(s)

A small networked sketch: a Player autoloaded on both server and client, the server is the node's set_multiplayer_authority, and an any_peer,call_local take_damage lets any client request damage while still applying it locally. The exact config a script registered is observable from GDScript via node.get_script().get_rpc_config() (a Dictionary keyed by method name → {rpc_mode, transfer_mode, call_local, channel}).

Host / join over ENet (the gd.* multiplayer helpers)#

godot/Ergonomics_Multiplayer.odin provides helpers to create an ENet peer, install it in the MultiplayerAPI, and receive connection callbacks. Each helper takes a node, such as a script's self.owner, and accesses its MultiplayerAPI through Node.get_multiplayer():

Odin
import gd "godot:godot"

// Host or join while the node is inside the tree. Each returns a
// bool so you can branch on failure (port in use, ENet unavailable on web, …):
@(gd_method)
player_host :: proc(self: ^Player, port: gd.Int) {
	if !gd.host(self.owner, int(port)) { gd.error("could not host"); return }
	gd.on_peer_connected(self.owner, "on_peer_joined")     // wire peer_connected -> method
	gd.on_peer_disconnected(self.owner, "on_peer_left")
}
@(gd_method)
player_join :: proc(self: ^Player, port: gd.Int) {
	gd.join(self.owner, "127.0.0.1", int(port))            // attempt; wait for connected_to_server
}

// Joined/left handlers (an @(gd_method) taking the peer id):
@(gd_method) on_peer_joined :: proc(self: ^Player, id: gd.Int) { /* spawn their avatar */ }
@(gd_method) on_peer_left   :: proc(self: ^Player, id: gd.Int) { /* despawn */ }

// Inside any @(gd_rpc), read who sent the call:
@(gd_method, gd_rpc = "any_peer")
player_chat :: proc(self: ^Player, msg: gd.String) {
	from := gd.rpc_sender_id(self.owner)                   // 0 for a local call_local dispatch
	_ = from
}
Task One-liner
Host an ENet server ok := gd.host(self.owner, 7777) (optional max_peers, default 32)
Join an ENet server ok := gd.join(self.owner, "127.0.0.1", 7777)
Am I the server/host? gd.is_server(self.owner)
My peer id id := gd.my_peer_id(self.owner) (server is always 1)
Sender of the current RPC gd.rpc_sender_id(self.owner) (call inside an @(gd_rpc))
All connected peer ids peers := gd.connected_peers(self.owner) ([]int, temp-allocated)
The MultiplayerAPI mp := gd.multiplayer(self.owner)
React to a peer joining/leaving gd.on_peer_connected(self.owner, "on_peer_joined") · gd.on_peer_disconnected(self.owner, "on_peer_left")

Web/WASM: Godot's web export does not ship ENetMultiplayerPeer, so gd.host/gd.join compile but return false on wasm32, so branch on the bool. For browser co-op use the WebRTC helpers below instead. The query helpers (is_server, my_peer_id, rpc_sender_id, connected_peers) are platform-independent and work over any peer (ENet or WebRTC).

tests/rpc_net runs a headless Godot server and client, connects them over ENet, and exchanges @(gd_rpc) calls in both directions. It checks that each call executes on the other peer with the correct get_remote_sender_id().

Launch parameters select an instance's role, relay, or room. Native launch scripts and the integration harness use environment variables; a browser instance can read the page URL's query string. gd.launch_param checks the environment first, then the web query parameter:

Odin
role := gd.launch_param("COOP_ROLE", "role")   // env COOP_ROLE, else ?role= on web
url  := gd.web_query("url")                     // web-only knob; "" on native

gd.web_query evaluates location.search through the JavaScriptBridge (values percent-decoded via gd.uri_decode); gd.IS_WEB is the compiled-for-the-browser constant the platform branches use. Results are temp-allocated. Both cooperative examples use these helpers during startup and exercise them in their native and browser integration tests.

WebRTC / web co-op (gd.webrtc_host / gd.webrtc_join)#

WebRTC supports browser multiplayer over the internet without port-forwarding. Godot exposes the browser's implementation through WebRTCMultiplayerPeer and WebRTCPeerConnection. godot/Ergonomics_WebRtc.odin opens a signaling channel, exchanges the SDP offer and answer, sends ICE connection candidates, creates data channels, and installs the peer. The game starts hosting or joining and polls the setup each frame:

Odin
// The host becomes peer id 1 and receives a room code for the joiner to use:
@(gd_method) lobby_host :: proc(self: ^Lobby) { gd.webrtc_host(self.owner, "wss://your-server/rtc") }
@(gd_method) lobby_join :: proc(self: ^Lobby) { gd.webrtc_join(self.owner, "wss://your-server/rtc", "WATR") }

// Poll signaling every frame until connected; later calls do no setup work:
lobby_process :: proc(self: ^Lobby, _delta: f64) {
    gd.webrtc_poll(self.owner)
    code := gd.webrtc_room_code(self.owner) // host: "" until the server assigns it — display to share
}

Once connected, the existing @(gd_rpc) methods and gd.rpc / gd.rpc_id calls use the WebRTC peer. Godot's RPC layer accepts a WebRTCMultiplayerPeer through the same MultiplayerPeer interface used for ENet, so the RPC declarations and calls can stay the same.

Task One-liner
Host a WebRTC lobby (id 1) ok := gd.webrtc_host(self.owner, "wss://host/rtc")
Join a WebRTC lobby by code ok := gd.webrtc_join(self.owner, "wss://host/rtc", "WATR")
Read the host's room code code := gd.webrtc_room_code(self.owner) ("" until assigned)
Signaling state / error gd.webrtc_session_state(...) / gd.webrtc_error_reason(...)
Pump signaling (every frame) gd.webrtc_poll(self.owner)
Tear the session down gd.webrtc_close(self.owner)

WebRTC needs a signaling server to exchange connection information before the peer-to-peer link exists. The host sends create and receives a room code; the other player sends join with that code. The server relays SDP offers, answers, and ICE candidates without parsing their contents. The protocol uses JSON text frames over a WebSocket at /rtc. A compatible server can implement the protocol below. The Node reference implementation at tests/webrtc/signal_server.mjs serves the headless tests; the maintainer uses an Elixir implementation in production.

Code
client -> server                                  server -> client
  {"type":"create"}                                 {"type":"created","room":"<CODE>","id":1}
  {"type":"join","room":"<CODE>"}                   {"type":"joined","room":"<CODE>","id":<n>}
  {"type":"signal","to":<peerId>,"data":<opaque>}   {"type":"peer","id":<peerId>}
  {"type":"leave"}                                  {"type":"signal","from":<peerId>,"data":<opaque>}
                                                    {"type":"peer_left","id":<peerId>}
                                                    {"type":"error","reason":"no_room"|"full"|"bad_msg"}

The host (id 1) creates the offer and the joiner answers. Both players must be able to reach the signaling server during setup, so deploy it at a public wss://HOST/rtc. Game traffic then uses WebRTC's peer-to-peer connection and NAT traversal without port-forwarding. Ergonomics_WebRtc .odin configures a public STUN server on the WebRTCPeerConnection. Add a TURN relay to _ICE_CONFIG_JSON for symmetric-NAT pairs; localhost needs neither STUN nor TURN.

Desktop/native Godot ships no WebRTC implementation: WebRTCPeer Connection is an abstract extension point ("No default WebRTC extension configured") that the separate godot-webrtc GDExtension must fill. These helpers target web exports. They compile and run natively, but initialize fails unless godot-webrtc is installed. Native extension setup is outside this guide's scope. tests/webrtc exercises the browser export.

tests/webrtc loads the same exported web page in two headless Chrome instances, one with ?role=host and one with ?role=join. They establish a browser-native WebRTC data channel through the signaling server and exchange @(gd_rpc) calls in both directions. Assertions in each browser's JS console check execution on the other browser with the correct sender id, matching the native checks in tests/rpc_net.

Godot helper procedures#

The godot/Ergonomics*.odin helpers create the StringName and Variant values and resolve the method bindings needed for common engine calls. Their Object/Node/Resource parameters and results share the representation used by object handles such as Node2d, Area2d, and Label. A script's self.owner therefore passes without a cast, and a returned Node assigns to another handle type.

Task One-liner
Resolve a child by path child := gd.get_node(self.owner, "Hud")
Get the parent node p := gd.get_parent(self.owner)
Get the SceneTree tree := gd.get_tree(self.owner)
Parent a node gd.add_child(self.owner, child)
Group add / check / remove gd.add_to_group(self.owner, "enemies") · gd.is_in_group(self.owner, "enemies") · gd.remove_from_group(self.owner, "enemies")
Iterate a group for n in gd.nodes_in_group(self.owner, "enemies") { ... } (live members, temp-allocated)
One group member game := gd.first_in_group(self.owner, "game")
Group → script structs for p in rt.scripts_in_group(self.owner, "players", player) { ... } · rt.first_script_in_group(self.owner, "game", Game) (see Typed cross-script references)
Unpack an engine array kids := gd.array_unpack(&children) (any Typed_Array return → Odin slice, element-converted)
Load a resource res := gd.load("res://icon.png")
Load a PackedScene scene := gd.load_scene("res://enemy.tscn")
Instance a PackedScene node := gd.instantiate(scene)
Load + instance + add_child enemy := gd.spawn(self.owner, "res://enemy.tscn")
Set a property by name gd.set_int/set_float/set_bool/set_string(obj, "value", v) · gd.set_value(obj, "p", variant)
Get a property by name gd.get_int/get_float/get_bool/get_string(obj, "value") · gd.get_value(obj, "p")
Connect own signal → own method gd.connect(self.owner, "body_entered", "collect")
Connect emitter → target method gd.connect_to(emitter, "sig", target, "method")
Build a bound Callable cb := gd.callable(self.owner, "method")
Emit a signal (no payload) gd.emit(self.owner, "died")
Emit a signal with payload v := i64(value); gd.emit_args(self.owner, "collected", gd.variant_from(&v))
Read a project setting gd.get_setting_int/float/bool/string("game/lives") · gd.get_setting("p") (raw Variant) · gd.get_setting_or("p", default)
Write a project setting gd.set_setting_int/float/bool/string("game/lives", v) · gd.set_setting("p", variant)
Has a project setting gd.has_setting("game/lives")
Define an input action gd.add_action("fire") (optional deadzone)
Bind a key / mouse button gd.action_add_key("fire", i64(gd.Key.Space)) · gd.action_add_mouse_button("fire", i64(gd.Mouse_Button.Left))
Has / erase an action gd.has_action("fire") · gd.erase_action("fire")
Poll an action gd.is_action_pressed("fire") · gd.is_action_just_pressed("jump") · gd.is_action_just_released("jump") · gd.get_action_strength("accelerate")
Movement input x := gd.get_axis("ui_left", "ui_right") · v := gd.get_vector("ui_left", "ui_right", "ui_up", "ui_down")
Synthesize input gd.action_press("fire", 0.8) · gd.action_release("fire")
Intern a name inline gd.sname("run") → String_Name · gd.gstr("text") → String (for raw calls with no gd.* wrapper)
Running in the editor? if gd.is_editor() { ... } (wraps Engine.is_editor_hint())
Set / get a control's text gd.set_text(self.label, "Score: 0") · s := gd.get_text(self.label) (any Control with a text property)
Play / stop an animation gd.animation_play(self.anim, "run") · gd.animation_stop(self.anim) · gd.is_animation_playing(self.anim)
Play / stop an AnimatedSprite2D gd.sprite_play(self.spr, "idle") · gd.sprite_stop(self.spr) · gd.is_sprite_playing(self.spr)
Play / stop audio gd.audio_play(self.sfx) · gd.audio_stop(self.sfx) (positional: gd.audio_play2d / gd.audio_stop2d)
Set one position component gd.node2d_set_x(self.owner, 100) (also node3d_* with _z, control_* with _width/_height; see Common 2D transforms)

gd.get_setting*/gd.set_setting* wrap the ProjectSettings singleton; gd.add_action / gd.action_add_* wrap the InputMap singleton (constructing the InputEventKey / InputEventMouseButton for you). Settings/actions registered at runtime are visible to GDScript (ProjectSettings.get_setting, InputMap.has_action, Input.is_action_pressed) but do not persist to project.godot. Register them during an autoload's _ready, as shown below. gd.get_setting_string allocates its returned string in context.allocator; the other setting and action helpers are proc "contextless".

All helpers are proc "contextless" except the ones that allocate: gd.get_string (returned Odin string, in context.allocator — delete it) and the slice-returning queries gd.nodes_in_group / gd.array_unpack / rt.scripts_in_group (in context.temp_allocator by default; iterate before the temporary storage is reset, or pass a persistent allocator to retain the slice). Script procedures run with a context set, so they can call either form. For a script-declared signal field, prefer the generated typed <struct_snake>_emit_<field> helper. Use gd.emit_args for by-name dispatch. Both gd.emit and emit_args use a Variant call because Godot's emit_signal is a vararg method and cannot use the pointer-call path.

The helpers above accept Odin cstrings and create the Godot String or String_Name internally. For a raw bound method without a helper, create those values with gd.sname("…") or gd.gstr("…"). Names for methods, signals, actions, animations, and properties usually take String_Name. The helper avoids spelling out new_string_name_cstring(…, true):

Odin
// raw call (no dedicated helper): intern the name inline
if gd.object_has_method(enemy, gd.sname("take_damage")) {
    // ...
}

gd.sname uses static = true (intern once, keep), correct for the string literals these calls almost always use.

Common 2D transforms — moving / rotating a Node2D#

gd.Vector2 is an Odin [2]f32, so it supports Odin's vector operations: component access (pos.x), compound assignment (pos.x += 10), and whole-vector arithmetic (pos += other, pos * delta). The only round-trip is the get/set across the engine boundary. For the common move, rotate, and scale operations, Godot provides methods that apply the delta directly:

Instead of (get → modify → set) One call
pos.x += 10 on the position gd.node2d_translate(self.owner, gd.Vector2{10, 0})
move along the node's own axes (respects rotation) gd.node2d_move_local_x(self.owner, 10) · gd.node2d_move_local_y(self.owner, 10)
rotate by radians gd.node2d_rotate(self.owner, 0.1)
scale by a factor gd.node2d_apply_scale(self.owner, gd.Vector2{2, 2})
set / get in world space gd.node2d_set_global_position(self.owner, p) · gd.node2d_get_global_position(self.owner)
set one position component (keep the other) gd.node2d_set_x(self.owner, 100) · gd.node2d_set_y(self.owner, 250) (and _global_x / _global_y)

The node2d_set_x / _set_y (+ _global_x / _global_y) helpers cover the absolute-component case ("snap x to 100, keep y") without a separate get, modify, and set. The same setters exist for other positional types: node3d_set_x/_y/_z (+ _global_*), and control_set_x/_y, control_set_width/_height, control_set_global_x/_y. If you ever need it by hand (a component with no setter, or another type), it's plain Odin array math:

Odin
pos := gd.node2d_get_position(self.owner)
pos.x = 100                                  // Odin array swizzle — no Vector2 ctor needed
gd.node2d_set_position(self.owner, pos)

Godot methods on nodes are bound as gd.<class_snake>_<method>(handle, args…) (so reach for node2d_translate, control_set_size, sprite2d_set_frame, …), and the math types (Vector2/3, Color, Rect2, …) are plain Odin structs/arrays you manipulate with normal operators.

Supported Odin → Variant types#

Odin type Variant Notes
int, i8/i16/i32/i64, u8..u64, uint, gd.Int Int width-narrowed via size_of
f32, f64, gd.Float, gd.Real Float
bool Bool
string String Method arguments/results are converted as UTF-8; use gd.String for exported storage.
gd.String String Engine value with explicit ownership.
gd.Vector2, gd.Vector3, gd.Color matching
gd.String_Name String_Name
^gd.<Object subclass>, gd.Node, gd.Object, ... Object object handle

Scriptgen rejects unsupported types with a build error. Raw gd.Variant signatures are not supported at this method boundary; use a concrete supported type or a lower-level Variant dispatch API.

Method value ownership#

Use ordinary Odin strings for textual method APIs:

Odin
@(gd_method)
player_echo :: proc(self: ^Player, text: string) -> string {return text}

The trampoline converts the incoming Godot String into temporary UTF-8 storage, copies returned text into the outgoing Variant, and releases its Godot argument copy when the call finishes. Keep returned storage valid until marshaling finishes: literals, instance-owned strings and context.temp_allocator data work; a view into a local stack array does not. Copy an argument with strings.clone if you retain it across frames. The trampoline does not free an Odin string you return from your own allocator.

A bare @(gd_method) uses these ownership rules: owning builtin argument copies belong to the callee, while returned Godot values are borrowed. The method must free its gd.String/gd.Array argument copies and may return an instance-owned value. Object-handle arguments are borrowed pointers, not owning builtin copies.

To change these ownership rules, add options to the attribute:

Odin
@(gd_method="borrowed_args,owned_return")
player_copy_values :: proc(self: ^Player, values: gd.Array) -> gd.Array {
    return gd.new_array_array(values)
}

@(gd_method="owned_return")
player_description :: proc(self: ^Player) -> gd.String {
    return gd.new_string_odin("Ready")
}

borrowed_args makes the trampoline release its builtin argument copies after the call. Treat those values as borrowed; use a Godot copy constructor before retaining or replacing a handle. A copied Array/Dictionary reference may still share mutable contents—ownership does not imply a deep copy.

owned_return transfers one owned builtin reference to the trampoline, which releases it after the outgoing Variant retains the value. It also supports a declared RefCounted subclass with one owned reference (factory results, or a new object after ref_counted_init_ref). It rejects Node/Object/scalar results; a Variant does not own a Node's lifetime. Native Odin string results already use the conversion path and do not take this option. Returning a borrowed argument as owned_return requires first acquiring a separate reference.

The options also follow composed methods and property accessors when the accessor proc has the annotated gd_method. Unannotated accessors use the default ownership rules. A String property's getter may return an Odin string, which is copied; its actual exported storage remains gd.String. Native string exports are rejected by scriptgen and reflection because their storage is not a Godot String.

Threads & memory#

Script callbacks use the engine thread and the allocators installed by the runtime:

  • Lifecycle procs (*_ready, *_process, …), @(gd_method) calls, @(gd_connect) handlers and @(gd_rpc) procs are all invoked by the engine on its main thread; the generated trampolines add no synchronization. Don't call gd.* / engine APIs from threads you spawn with core:thread: compute on the worker, then apply the result back on the main thread from a lifecycle proc (e.g. poll a mutex-guarded value in *_process).
  • rt.script_of is main-thread-only: it resolves through the core's live-instance registry, which the main thread mutates as script instances are created and freed.
  • context.allocator is persistent inside script procedures: the Odin heap default on native, an engine-backed (alignment-correct) allocator on web. Either way, what you make/new there lives until you free it.
  • context.temp_allocator supplies temporary storage. The core resets its shared temp arena once per frame from the main-thread frame pump, so never stash a temp pointer (including fmt.tprintf/fmt.ctprintf results) across frames. Copy anything you keep into context.allocator memory.
  • The caller frees strings allocated by gd.get_string and helpers like it that return an Odin string. They allocate from context.allocator; use delete(s) when you're done with it.
  • gd.sname uses new_string_name_cstring(name, true): static = true hands Godot the cstring pointer to keep for the program's lifetime. Pass only string literals (or otherwise program-lifetime, ASCII) names; never a name built at runtime from a temporary buffer such as fmt.ctprintf(...).

Building#

build/build_scripts.sh [PROJECT_DIR] runs the full pipeline:

  1. builds the scriptgen binary,
  2. runs scriptgen <scriptsdir> to emit the build artifacts beside the authored sources (one odin_godot_scripts.gen.odin per package directory, plus the scripts dir's staleness guard and boot shim; no resource stubs, since the authored .odin is the attached resource),
  3. builds the scripts dll with odin build <scriptsdir> -build-mode:dll -custom-attribute:gd_method -custom-attribute:gd_connect -custom-attribute:gd_rpc -custom-attribute:gd_command -custom-attribute:gd_tick -custom-attribute:gd_input -custom-attribute:gd_sample -custom-attribute:gd_step -custom-attribute:gd_event -custom-attribute:gd_half -custom-attribute:gd_message (the .gen.odin are in the same package and compile together),
  4. builds the core dll.

The eleven -custom-attribute: flags are required so the Odin compiler accepts the @(gd_method) / @(gd_connect) / @(gd_rpc) / @(gd_command) / @(gd_tick) / @(gd_input) / @(gd_sample) / @(gd_step) / @(gd_event) / @(gd_half) / @(gd_message) marker attributes; the build script passes them for you. The set lives in decl/decl.odin's ATTRS, and tests/scriptgen checks that the build scripts pass those attributes. Odin rejects an unknown custom attribute, so adding one to the schema also requires updating the build scripts.

Workflow covers builds, live editing with updates on save, validation, autocomplete, highlighting, debugging, and editor settings such as odin_godot/odin_bin and odin_godot/scripts_dir.

Multiple scripts in one package#

All the .odin files in one directory are one Odin package. Because lifecycle/method procs and generated emit helpers live in that shared package, prefix your proc names with the struct name (ping_ready, ping_add) to avoid collisions, since the prefix is stripped to derive the GDScript-facing name. One script struct per file (identified by its first field being named owner).

Organizing a project#

Start with one res://scripts/ directory. Split out packages when the directory becomes hard to navigate, and consider modules when rebuild latency warrants separate libraries:

Shape Use it for Cost
flat res://scripts/ everything, until a directory listing gets hard to read none; this is the default
a helper subpackage (scripts/util/, no annotated scripts in it) pure Odin logic with no engine surface: math, parsers, tables. Import it relatively (import "util") none; it compiles into the same dll
a script subpackage (scripts/ui/, with annotated scripts) self-contained engine-native classes the rest of the game does not need to name: HUD widgets, menus, tools, effects. They attach from their own path (res://scripts/ui/hud.odin) kit declarations must stay in the top-level scripts dir, and a subpackage may not import it back. Still one dll, so a save still rebuilds all of it
a script module (res://modules/<name>/) a subsystem whose rebuild latency warrants a separate library (hundreds of scripts) its own dll, so no shared types or globals with other modules: cross-module calls go through the engine
res://shared/ types, constants and pure procs several modules must agree on verified state-free (no mutable globals, no @(init), no scripts), and an edit there rebuilds every module

The last three are covered in Script Modules, including the cost model, the isolation rule, and the exact build-time refusals.

Custom resources#

//gd:extends Resource attaches the script to a custom resource, a RefCounted data container outside the scene tree, like GDScript's extends Resource. Use it for designer-tunable data assets you create, edit in the Inspector, and save as .tres.

Odin
//gd:extends Resource
//gd:class ItemData
package game_scripts

import gd "godot:godot"

ItemData :: struct {
	owner: gd.Resource,
	name:  gd.String   `gd:"export"`,
	value: gd.Int      `gd:"export,range=0:999"`,
	icon:  ^gd.Resource `gd:"export,resource=Texture2D"`,
}

@(gd_method)
item_data_item_total :: proc(self: ^ItemData) -> int {
	return int(self.value) + 100
}

  • No lifecycle. A resource is not in the scene tree, so _ready / _process / _physics_process never fire, so omit them. @export vars and @(gd_method)s work as usual.

  • First field is owner: gd.Resource (the owner-Object convention), instead of a gd.Node/gd.Node2d.

  • .tres serialization is automatic. @export vars carry the STORAGE usage flag, so Godot's own text-resource serializer writes them (plus a reference to this script) into a .tres. Loading the .tres reconstructs a live instance with the script re-attached, so its methods still dispatch:

    GDScript
    var item = Resource.new()
item.set_script(load("res://scripts/item_data.odin"))
item.set("name", "Sword"); item.set("value", 10)
ResourceSaver.save(item, "res://sword.tres")

var loaded = ResourceLoader.load("res://sword.tres")
loaded.get("value")        # 10
loaded.call("item_total")  # 110 — script re-bound on load

    The saved .tres is plain Godot text:

    Code
    [gd_resource type="Resource" format=3]
[ext_resource type="Script" path="res://scripts/item_data.odin" id="1_x"]
[resource]
script = ExtResource("1_x")
name = "Sword"
value = 10

  • Editable in the editor. Unlike a non-tool node script (which the editor shows via a read-only placeholder), attaching a resource script builds a real, live instance even in the editor, so its @export values are directly editable in the Inspector and persist on save.

  • Resource-typed @export. A field data: ^gd.Resource gd:"export,resource=ItemData"`` on a node script gives a resource-picker slot that accepts a custom ItemData .tres. The resource= hint string filters the picker, and because ItemData is registered as a global class (see below) the editor knows it as a type.

Global class names#

//gd:class <Name> registers the script as a global class, like GDScript's class_name. The declared name becomes the engine's global name without another annotation.

The marker is optional. Without it, the script still attaches, instantiates, reloads, and supports typed rt.script_of access through its source-path identity. It does not reserve a project-wide global type name. Use it when another editor surface needs a named type (for example a custom Resource picker), not as routine binding boilerplate. The editor's new-script template therefore leaves it out by default.

  • Script.get_global_name() returns <Name> (this is ScriptExtension._get_global_name, the virtual the editor's filesystem scan reads).
  • After the editor scans the project, <Name> appears in ProjectSettings.get_global_class_list() with its declared native base_type (from //gd:extends), so the engine treats it as a usable type and a type-filter (e.g. a resource/node-typed @export picker).

The registration is driven by the language's _handles_global_class_type / _get_global_class_name(path) virtuals, which reparse the .odin file's markers and hand back {name, base_type, icon_path}.

Typed cross-script references#

All scripts in a module compile into one shared library, so they can use the same struct types. rt.script_of(obj, T) resolves a live Godot object to a typed ^T pointer to its Odin script data. Scripts in that module can then access fields and call procedures directly without Variant marshaling:

Odin
import gd "godot:godot"
import rt "godot:runtime"

@(gd_method)
controller_attack :: proc(self: ^Controller, amount: gd.Int) -> int {
	target := gd.get_node(self.owner, "Enemy")  // or an @export node ref
	enemy := rt.script_of(target, Enemy)         // -> ^Enemy (nil if not an Odin Enemy)
	if enemy == nil { return -1 }
	enemy.hp -= amount       // direct typed field write
	enemy_heal(enemy, 0)     // direct typed proc call
	return int(enemy.hp)
}
  • script_of returns nil when obj is nil or carries no Odin script of our language (a foreign-language node, a placeholder, or a plain engine node). It is safe to call with a nil object.
  • Works on web too (single module: the same resolver is wired directly).
  • Subpackages are not a boundary: a class in a subfolder of the same module lives in the same dll, so import that package and name its type: rt.script_of(node, ui.Hud).
  • Module boundary: if the project uses script modules, script_of is typed access within one module only: across modules it returns nil by construction (modules can't import each other's types), and cross-module access goes through the engine (signals, name-based calls, autoloads). See Script Modules.
  • For calling across a dll boundary (e.g. a tool that dispatches by name), the GDScript-style by-name path is gd.vcall (below); script_of provides direct typed path within the shared scripts dll.

These three helpers combine scene instantiation and typed script lookup. Choose one according to whether the new instance's _ready needs to see the initial field values:

Odin
// Set initial fields before _ready with spawn_scripted + add_child:
node, b := rt.spawn_scripted(self.bullet_scene, Bullet)
if b == nil { return }
b.dir = dir; b.damage = dmg
gd.add_child(arena, node)

// Assign fields after _ready has run:
if e := rt.spawn_as(parent, self.enemy_scene, Enemy); e != nil { e.tier = 2 }

// from a physics callback (body_entered, contact resolution): deferred parenting —
// _ready runs at idle time and sees assignments through the returned ^T.
if g := rt.spawn_as_deferred(parent, self.gem_scene, Gem); g != nil { g.value = 5 }

All are nil-safe (nil scene, failed instantiate, or a root without the expected script → nil ^T; the caller's nil-check decides whether that's fatal).

Where types cannot be shared, such as across script modules or through engine-mediated dispatch, gd.vcall converts Odin arguments to Variants automatically, calls by name, and frees every temporary; the typed forms unwrap the result:

Odin
gd.vcall_void(spawner, "register_kill")
hits := gd.vcall_int(field, "spawn_aimed", x, y, sx, sy, speed, dmg, gd.Int(1))
if gd.vcall_bool(game_state, "is_cleared") { ... }

Accepted argument types: integers, floats, bool, cstring/string, gd.String, gd.String_Name, object/node handles, Vector2/2i/3/3i/4, Color, Rect2, and prebuilt Variants, which pass through with ownership retained by the caller. An unsupported argument rejects the entire call and reports an error. A nil target is a silent no-op returning zero, which supports group or path lookups that find no object. method must be an interned string literal.

Use scene-tree groups to find nodes without retaining their paths or a separate registry. Add nodes with gd.add_to_group in _ready, then use the rt queries to resolve group members through script_of. The queries return script pointers and skip members that carry a different script or no script:

Odin
// Find players through a temporary slice of struct pointers; iterate before it resets:
for p in rt.scripts_in_group(self.owner, "players", player) {
	p.hp -= 1                                     // direct field access
	pos := gd.node2d_get_global_position(p.owner) // engine calls via the owner
}

// the single-expected-object query (the game orchestrator, the world, the camera):
game := rt.first_script_in_group(self.owner, "game", Game)

first_script_in_group scans until it finds a member with the requested script. Calling gd.first_in_group and then script_of instead checks only the first node listed by the engine. The node-level forms (gd.nodes_in_group, gd.first_in_group) and the generic engine-array unpacker (gd.array_unpack) live in the ergonomics layer. One timing note: nodes join groups as they enter the tree, so a group scan inside another node's _ready can run before later siblings have registered. Query from process or tick code when the game needs the result.

Any-class references & static dispatch ("interfaces")#

Use script_of when the expected class is known. For a bullet that can damage several classes, or a cursor that can interact with several classes, rt.script_any(obj) -> (ptr: rawptr, id: typeid) returns the instance data and its type. It returns nil,nil for a plain engine node, a foreign module's class, or an object without a script.

A static table can map each typeid to the operations that class supports. Each entry applies to every instance of its class, so the game needs no per-instance registration or teardown. This explicitly represents a dispatch table similar to a C++ or C# vtable:

Odin
Damage_Entry :: struct {
	id:   typeid,
	hurt: proc(ctx: rawptr, amount: int),
}

DAMAGE_IMPLS := [?]Damage_Entry {
	{typeid_of(bug),    proc(ctx: rawptr, n: int) {bug_take_damage(cast(^bug)ctx, n)}},
	{typeid_of(cactus), proc(ctx: rawptr, n: int) {cactus_smash(cast(^cactus)ctx)}},
}

// the one call site every projectile shares:
hurt :: proc(node: gd.Object, amount: int) -> bool {
	if d, ptr, ok := rt.dispatch(DAMAGE_IMPLS[:], node); ok {
		d.hurt(ptr, amount)
		return true
	}
	return false
}

rt.dispatch(table, obj) composes the resolve and the table scan; rt.lookup(table, id) is the scan alone (for call sites that must distinguish "not a script" from "no entry", or that already hold the typeid). Both are generic on the entry type: any struct with an id: typeid field works, checked at instantiation. INTERACT_IMPLS and SAVE_IMPLS can therefore use their own entry structs without a shared header or a requirement that id come first. [:] converts the table from an array to a slice ([2]Damage_Entry → []Damage_Entry), and the $E parameter accepts different entry types. The compiler checks both the slice and entry types.

The [?] literal is initialized as constant data in the binary. A package-global map[typeid] instead needs allocation during library loading, when the web target's allocator is not yet usable; see runtime/context.odin. Scriptgen's generated tables use [?] arrays for the same reason. A short contiguous scan also avoids hash-table overhead for small sets. If the table outgrows a scan or needs per-file registration, initialize a map lazily inside the dispatch procedure on its first call after boot.

Procedure literals must be capture-free because Odin has no closures. Pass the instance through ctx. The core reports the instance's class name, and script_any resolves it through the current library's registry to a typeid. A class from an unregistered module resolves to nil, preventing access through an incompatible struct layout. Like script_of, these queries require the main thread and work on web through a directly wired resolver.

For a closed set whose callers need type-specific behavior, a tagged union such as union {^bug, ^cactus} with an exhaustive switch lets the compiler check that each type is handled. Use the table when N types share one operation; use the union when callers need exhaustive case analysis.

For a global score or constant table without a per-node instance, use file-private variables and package procedures such as game_state_add. Scripts in one directory share an Odin package and can access that state directly. Package state has no /root/Name node, GDScript visibility, or _ready callback. Use an autoload when a manager needs those engine features or persistence across scene changes.

Autoload singletons#

A .odin script can be a Godot autoload singleton: a node added under /root at startup, reachable everywhere (from GDScript as Name or /root/Name, from Odin via gd.get_node on any node's tree), persistent across scene changes, running _ready once.

Write a normal script whose base is a Node (or any Node subclass), give it a //gd:class name, and add it to project.godot's [autoload] section with a leading *:

Odin
